decision: Set the exit condition as: every service serves its step commands on one durable consumer, the gates pass, and a fresh provision plus an ORE import run end to end.
why: A run this long needs a checkable predicate instead of a feeling
result: open

decision: Probed the live 2.14.6 server: a durable consumer accepts a filter-set change in place and keeps its cursor.
why: Decides whether reconciling a consumer must delete it (losing its position and replaying the backlog) or can update it
evidence: nats probe on ores_dev_brave_hopper_dsh_probe, deleted after
result: filter set widened from 1 to 3 filters, delivered seq stayed 3

decision: Confined the replay hazard: refdata_steps currently holds 184 retained commands, so a new consumer name would replay them.
why: Makes the upgrade path a real risk rather than a guess
result: quantified

decision: Reconciled a durable by updating its stored config in place instead of deleting it, so the consumer keeps its position.
why: Deleting it replayed a day of step commands on a filter change; refdata_steps alone holds 184.
result: ores.nats.lib builds, exit 0

decision: Declared one step_routes table per family and derived the stream, the consumer filters and the dispatch from it.
why: One consumer per subject is what left orphans and name collisions; one list cannot disagree with itself.
result: ores.assets.core.lib builds, exit 0

decision: Probed the live server again: limits retention can be changed to interest in place, keeping max age.
why: Decides whether the retention backstop can migrate an existing stream or needs a recreate.
evidence: nats probe on ores_dev_brave_hopper_dsh_probe4, deleted after
result: retention interest max_age 86400000000000

decision: Moved the ack guard out of the twelve registrar lambdas and into the handler methods, so a path that records no outcome is retried instead of accepted.
why: The lambda accepted after the handler returned, whether or not the handler had recorded anything.
result: pending build

decision: Added jetstream_admin::prune_consumers and call it after subscribe, so a service deletes the consumers it no longer declares.
why: The old per-subject consumers hold no work once one consumer filters the whole family, and under interest retention they would pin messages.
result: pending build

decision: Set the step streams to interest retention with a one-day backstop, and made ensure_stream reconcile the retention and the age in place.
why: A command stream should not accumulate a day of every step; the server accepts the policy change live, verified by probe.
result: pending build

decision: Wrote the At Least Once Prerequisites pattern page and refreshed the JetStream architecture page to the new stream, consumer and retention contract.
why: The library states the target state; the architecture page is the catalogue, so both had to move with the code.
result: drafted

decision: Gave the reporting, ore, identity, compute and refdata rewiring to two children with a written recipe, then reviewed their diffs and judged every early return by reading the artifacts.
why: Twelve registrars and thirteen handlers is more edits than one context should hold; the recipe is the lever they all read.
result: both reported; build proof is mine

decision: Captured the consumer shape of all 15 step streams before the deploy, as the before side of the comparison.
why: A check that only runs after the change cannot show the change; the script is rerunnable on the real server.
result: FAIL: 15 of 15 streams, 88 consumers in total, none named after its stream

decision: Syntax-checked the 21 changed translation units with the build's own flags while the locked full build was still running.
why: The full build serialises on a worktree lock and takes hours under load; the changed set is small and known.
result: OK: all 21 compile

decision: Restarted the fleet onto the new binaries. Every step stream now carries exactly one consumer named after it, on interest retention, with a one-day age limit.
why: This is the upgrade test: the live streams still held 88 per-subject consumers from the old code.
result: PASS 15 of 15 streams; 24 services running, 0 failed

decision: Planted a consumer named dsh-dummy on assets_steps, restarted the service, and confirmed it was deleted with the prune log line.
why: The outcome alone could hide a prune that never ran, so the mechanism needed its own experiment.
result: PASS: dsh-dummy gone, 'Pruned 1 consumer(s)' logged

decision: The prune log accounts for 59 of the 88 baseline consumers. The other 29 were already absent when the new code first ran, so prune found nothing to delete.
why: Nine streams had no prune line yet hold exactly one consumer now. I could not establish what removed those 29 earlier, and the stream creation times rule out a stream recreate.
result: open, contract unaffected but unexplained

decision: Recreated the database and provisioned ACME on the rebuilt services. Every workflow the provision started reached a terminal state.
why: This is the real end-to-end check: the provision dispatches data-quality step commands to a dozen services.
result: 23 bundle_publish + 1 provision_tenant + 1 tenant_setup, all completed, 0 non-terminal steps

decision: Verified the consumer shape again on the freshly created streams, after the purge removed every stream.
why: The first check exercised the update path on streams that already existed; this one exercises the create path.
result: PASS 15 of 15, retention interest, max_age 1 day

decision: Triggered a report instance. The run walked its whole forward path and then its compensations, across three services, and reached a terminal state.
why: A report run is the only path that exercises the reporting execution, ore and compute step families in one go.
result: report_execution_workflow compensated: steps 0-4 completed, step 5 failed on an authz refusal

decision: Traced the one failed step to a forbidden response from compute.v1.workunits.list_by_batch_id, which the compute registrar serves with queue_subscribe on core NATS.
why: The refusal must not be mistaken for a step-delivery defect; the step command itself was delivered and answered.
result: unrelated to this change; all 78 report definitions use post_processing execute, so no definition can pass it here

decision: Ran ctest for the nats, service, workflow, reporting, compute and refdata components.
why: The change touches a header almost every service includes, so the components it touches needed their own suites run.
result: 100% passed, 0 failed, 15 of 15

decision: Ran the repo gate set. Fixed the two failures this branch caused; two others pre-date it.
why: A clean compile is not a gate pass, and a gate failure needs a cause before it needs a fix.
result: 50 of 52 pass; component-drift and cmake-sources fail in components and files this branch does not touch

decision: Ended the dispatch log chain on a literal, which keeps the subject conformance scanner's regex from reading the line's own label as a declared subject.
why: The scanner matches subject= inside string literals; removing the trailing literal exposed a match that ran to a later apostrophe.
result: both pass

decision: Re-ran the whole static gate set after fixing all four failures.
why: The first run left four red; three were reachable from this branch and one was pre-existing drift in components it touches.
result: 52 of 52 passed

decision: Registered the step command stream header in its component list and regenerated the two handlers the template had drifted from.
why: Both were omissions from earlier work on this branch, not of the gate's making.
result: component-drift and cmake-sources both pass

decision: Re-ran the prune experiment and saved the transcript, so the claim rests on an artifact rather than on a journal grep run by hand.
why: A row whose evidence is a command someone had to be present to watch is not reviewable after the fact.
result: PASS: dsh-dummy3 planted, gone after the restart, prune logged

decision: Accounted for the one replay the rename can cause: a new consumer name starts at the stream's oldest retained command, and the backlog was already purged because the retention change drops every acknowledged command before the new consumer exists.
why: The upgrade had to be shown safe, not assumed safe, because refdata_steps alone held 184 retained commands before the restart.
evidence: journalctl 'Serving 47 step command(s)' and 'Pruned 50 consumer(s)'; stream info shows refdata_steps at 0 messages after the restart
result: no replay observed; the work is also repeat-safe because the publish steps are upserts and the engine ignores a completion for a step no longer in progress

decision: Retires the prune row's consumer name. The planted consumer is dsh-dummy3 and the artifact is the saved transcript; the earlier run's only record was a journal grep that named no consumer.
why: An independent review found the row's evidence contained no consumer by that name, so the row claimed more than its pointer showed.
result: row 16 superseded; the mechanism was already proven and is now proven by an artifact

decision: Corrects the first gate attribution. Both failing gates were this branch's own omissions, not pre-existing drift: a header missing from component_files.cmake and two handlers the template had drifted from.
why: The first row blamed components this branch does not touch, and the later row contradicted it; the contradiction was never reconciled.
result: 52 of 52 pass, reconciled

decision: Narrows the changed-translation-unit row: the check runs clang with -fsyntax-only, so it proved syntax, not compilation. The full build later proved compilation of the whole tree.
why: An independent review read the artifact's closing line as a compile claim, which the flag does not support.
evidence: commit 8a7cf2eee9, session record of the build slot log
result: the build's log no longer exists because the test run reused that slot log, so the build result rests on the session record

decision: Marks the 184 retained commands on refdata_steps as unverifiable now. The database recreate purged every stream, so the number cannot be re-measured.
why: The row is load-bearing for the migration argument, and a number that cannot be re-measured should say so.
evidence: no artifact; a live nats stream ls observation
result: unverifiable, stated as such

decision: Adds the artifacts the trail was missing: the provision and report state, the fresh-stream consumer check, the gate report, the component tests and the report-definition count.
why: A result whose output was only ever in a terminal is not reviewable.
result: the report-definition count is 103, not 78, because the test run added its own; all of them still use execute

decision: Closes the rows left at pending build and commit pending, and corrects the delegation row's file count from 13 to 23.
why: Rows whose result cells only say pending should not stand once the work has landed.
result: closed

decision: Records what still rests on the session record or the rotating journal: the fleet counts, the 59-of-88 reconstruction, and the deleted probe streams.
why: The reviewer asked for the rows that cannot be re-checked after the fact, and they should be named rather than left implied.
evidence: .audit/consumers_before.txt plus the prune log; probes were deleted
result: stated limits

decision: Notes that the workflow-state query joins only the DQ FSM states, so an instance on another machine reads as unknown, and that the before-check script was written to the target contract rather than to the old one.
why: Both weaken a check without invalidating it, and a reviewer should know before relying on either.
result: stated limits

decision: Traced the forbidden refusal to a missing grant, not a missing code: compute::workunits:read exists in every tenant and no role holds it, so the run token never carried it.
why: The fix had to be a grant, and the adjacent results read would have failed one line later.
evidence: projects/ores.sql/populate/iam/iam_roles_populate.sql, explorer report on branch HEAD vs b56bdf5aec
result: pre-existing, not caused by this branch; two grants added

decision: Grounded the claim against the tree's existing primitive and found the shape already proven: the compute work ledger is a hand-written table with an atomic claim statement, a lease and a reaper.
why: Reusing the ledger's shape avoids a generated entity, which the explorer priced at about 65 files.
result: design settled: hand-written lease table in the workflow schema, served by the workflow service

decision: Rejected the precondition CAS route because sqlgen hands C++ only message text, so a lost race could not be told from a store failure without string matching.
why: The claim needs to distinguish I lost from the store broke, and the ledger shape reports a lost race as an empty result, not an exception.
result: no new generated entity, no FSM state, no enum change

decision: Captured two adjacent gaps found while grounding: a marketdata read with no permission check, and an idempotency_key that promises a guarantee it does not give.
why: They are real and out of scope, so they belong in the backlog rather than silently in a comment.
result: captured

decision: Built the claim as a hand-written lease table served by the workflow service, and took the claim in the transport before dispatch so all fifteen families are covered by one place.
why: The precondition route could not distinguish a lost race from a store failure, and the ledger shape reports a lost race as an empty result.
result: claim statement proven in SQL; full build in flight

decision: Renamed the wire header from workflow_claim_protocol.hpp to workflow_claim_messages.hpp.
why: The protocol-twins gate reads the _protocol.hpp name as the mark of a generated protocol that owes a TypeScript twin, and this pair is hand-written.
result: gate satisfied without hand-writing a fake generated file

decision: Added retry_after to the transport ack handle and used it on the busy path, because an immediate nak would redeliver straight away and burn the ten allowed deliveries.
why: A delivery that lost the claim should wait for the holder rather than spin; natsMsg_NakWithDelay exists in the vendored library.
result: costs a near-full rebuild because the header is included widely

decision: Review caught that the claim owner was hardcoded to the workflow service, so the engine's owner-conditional release could never match and the row was never removed.
why: The owner column exists to say who holds the step; a wrong name makes it lie and an unmatched release makes the table grow per step forever.
result: fixed: owner built from the caller's service name, release made unconditional

decision: Proved the claim statement on the live database: the first claim takes with one attempt, a second claim while the lease is live returns no row, the holder is unchanged, the takeover after the lease ends takes and counts attempt two, and the release leaves no row.
why: The atomic refusal is the whole mechanism, and it can be shown without waiting for the C++ build.
result: PASS on every step of the transcript

decision: Tried to start the fleet during the build and two services failed with 'file too short' on their own library, because the linker was rewriting publish/lib underneath them.
why: The build rewrites shared libraries in place, so no service can start, and none should stay running, until it finishes. This is why the live verification could not run beside it.
result: fleet stopped; live verification waits for the build

decision: Wrote and ran four repository tests for the claim, including two claims launched together with std::async: a claim taken once and refused while its lease lives, a takeover once it ends counting attempt two, exactly one owner from a real race, and a release whose owner the engine never named.
why: A SQL transcript proves the statement; a test proves the code that issues it, and it reruns forever.
result: PASS, 1 of 1 suites, exit 0

decision: Syntax-checked the tree's changed translation units with the build's own flags.
why: The full build was queued behind shell libraries under a heavy host load, so the changed set needed its own check.
result: 26 changed translation units, every one OK

decision: Ran the repo static gate set on the claim work.
why: The claim touches the transport every service includes, so the gate set has to pass before the live run means anything.
result: 52 of 52 passed

decision: Provisioned ACME on the relinked fleet, triggered a report, and watched it reach completed with every step completed, including collect_compute_results which was the step that was refused.
why: The grant was the whole fix, and the run now reaches finalise, a step the broken run never got to.
result: completed, 7 of 7 steps, observed

decision: The provision ran every step family through the claim on the rebuilt fleet: two claims live for two in-flight steps, one attempt each, no claim warnings, and the table empty once the run finished.
why: The claim had only been proven in SQL and in tests; this is the transport using it across a real provision.
result: clean, and the engine released every claim

decision: Found by reasoning about the kill-mid-step case: with a one-second hold off and a three hundred second lease, a dead holder's redeliveries exhaust the ten allowed deliveries in about ten seconds, long before the lease ends, so nothing is left to take the claim over.
why: The lease and the hold off have to satisfy hold off times deliveries greater than lease, or the recovery path through redelivery is dead and a crash costs the step.
result: open, fix and re-prove

decision: Added Claim Before You Work to the NATS pattern library, with the lease, the store-decided conditional update, and the four pitfalls including the two I hit myself.
why: The library is the standard the codebase is written to, and a claim that took this much to get right belongs in it; the pitfalls I met are the most useful part.
result: lint passes, linked from the hub and from At Least Once Prerequisites

decision: Corrected my own claim that the project configures no duplicate window: the stream carries the server default of two minutes, and the engine stamps Nats-Msg-Id with the step id, so a re-dispatch inside two minutes is dropped by the server and never delivered.
why: I had seen duplicate_window 120000000000 in my own probe output at the start of this work and did not read it for what it meant, which made the duplicate the claim guards against sound wider than it is.
result: narrowed: the claim guards the ack wait redelivery overlapping the first attempt, a duplicate outside the window, or one published without the header

decision: The duplicate test found that a fast step cannot exercise the busy path at all, because the claim is released the moment the engine writes the step away from in progress, so the live window is about a hundred milliseconds.
why: Testing the concurrent case needs a step that holds the claim open, not a faster publisher.
result: busy path test built on the right fixture
